concept.name: Layer 1
concept.definition: A layer 1 (L1) is the base blockchain network itself — such as Ethereum or Bitcoin — that provides its own consensus, data availability and settlement, and on which layer-2 systems anchor their security.
concept.intuition: The L1 is the bedrock courthouse of record: slower and expensive, but its rulings are final and everything built above ultimately defers to it.
concept.mechanics: L1s execute and validate all transactions directly on the base chain, so throughput is bounded by what ordinary nodes can process; scaling the L1 itself (onchain scaling) requires protocol changes. Layer-2 rollups move execution off the L1 but post transaction data or proofs back to it, inheriting its security and finality.
concept.failure_modes: L1 congestion prices out users and pushes activity to less secure venues; a consensus failure or successful attack on the L1 undermines every layer 2 anchored to it.
concept.misconceptions: Not every chain with cheap fees is 'just an L2' — sidechains with their own consensus are separate L1-style systems that do not inherit Ethereum's security. L1 scaling by simply raising block size sacrifices decentralization.
concept.example: Ethereum Mainnet is the L1 that processes ~15M gas of target block usage per 12-second slot; Arbitrum posts its transaction batches to Ethereum so that, even if Arbitrum's operator vanishes, users can reconstruct state and exit via the L1.
